title: Architectural Trade-Offs in a Real-Time AI Transcription Assistant: An Evidence-Guided Case Study
content: Background: Real-time AI information systems increasingly combine local speech processing, remote language-model inference, interactive state, and persistence within one workflow. The resulting engineering problem is partly architectural: reliability and maintainability depend on how computational, protocol, and state boundaries are defined. Objective: I examine how those boundaries are implemented in a real-time AI transcription assistant and identify trade-offs and failure modes that are not visible in a component-level architecture alone. Methods: I performed a single-case, artifact-grounded architectural study using an architecture specification, a code-level walkthrough, and execution-oriented implementation traces. I reconstructed dependencies, traced representative workflows, examined model and state lifecycles, and inspected error and persistence semantics. Results: The case implements two runtime processes and a three-layer responsibility structure, process-local lazy speech-model initialization, a voice-activity-driven utterance state machine, cloud LLM inference through synchronous and streaming interfaces, and JSON-framed server-sent events. The analysis identifies four recurring architectural tensions: process separation versus duplicated model state; permissive contracts versus semantic validation; stream framing versus end-to-end error semantics; and availability-oriented persistence versus audit completeness. Conclusion: The study contributes an evidence-guided architectural account and a set of case-derived, testable propositions that clarify how boundary decisions shape real-time AI information systems.
